title: Peh

lines: MOSES: I AM SLOW OF SPEECH.
I WILL BE WITH YOUR MOUTH.
cards: Moses stands at the burning bush with one more objection, and this one is about his mouth. He tells God he has never been a man of words; he is slow of speech and slow of tongue.

A toast, a phone call, a hard conversation: the excuse has a familiar shape. God answers with a question, who made a person's mouth, and then a promise: I will be with your mouth, and teach you what to say.
The man whose words fill so much of the Torah starts out afraid to open his.

teach.h: PEH: A MOUTH, WITH SOMETHING INSIDE.
teach.b: Peh means a mouth, and the letter makes a p or an f, the sounds your lips make. Four ways to open it. First, the shape.

A printed peh can look like a mouth, curved open, with a small mark tucked inside. Some teachers say it's a tongue, waiting. Others say it's a reminder that a mouth holds something back as well as letting it out.
Second, Moses. He thinks his mouth disqualifies him. God doesn't argue that he speaks well.
God says the mouth was made, and help will come into it. Third, prayer. The Amidah, the standing prayer, is opened with a short line from the Psalms.

teach.h: OPEN MY LIPS BEFORE THE AMIDAH.
teach.b: In the King James words: "O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise." The Talmud discusses saying it there. Before the prayer's own words begin, a person asks for help just to open their mouth.
Another psalm asks God to set a watch before the mouth and keep the door of the lips.
Jewish ethics has a whole body of law about speech, lashon hara, the evil tongue, warning against harmful talk about others even when it's true.

teach.h: O LORD, OPEN THOU MY LIPS.
teach.b: So the mouth here is a door. It opens for praise, teaching and comfort, and it has a doorkeeper. The same peh that can bless can wound, and the tradition takes both seriously.
Moses's slow mouth ended up carrying words people still read aloud.

how: Jews open the Amidah, the central standing prayer, with the verse from Psalm 51 asking God to open their lips; Jewish law on speech, lashon hara, guards against harmful talk about others.

o: an open door, the letter of welcome
a mouth, the letter your lips make
a tooth, the letter of chewing

p: slow of speech and slow of tongue

s: Moses tells God he is a gifted speaker
he says he is slow of speech and slow of tongue.
the Amidah is opened with a verse asking God to open the lips
it warns against harmful talk about others even when it's true.

games.q: you're Moses at the bush. God is sending you to Pharaoh, and you're afraid of your own mouth. what does God say in the story?
o: that Moses is actually a fine speaker.
who made a person's mouth? I will be with your mouth.
that Moses doesn't need to speak at all.
games.why: God doesn't flatter him. the answer is that the mouth was made, and help will come into it.

practice: Close your mouth gently and breathe through your nose for a few breaths, noticing how rarely your mouth rests.
Then bring to mind one person who would be glad to hear something kind from you, and find the words: true, small and specific, not you're great, but the way you handled that meeting was brave.
If you pray, you can ask for help opening your lips.

wordCard.voice: Peh. A mouth: the letter of the lips, of Moses's slow speech, and of the line said before the Amidah. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: mouth. The name of the letter, which makes the sound of the lips.

carryVoice: Your line: peh is a mouth. The same door can bless or wound. Same time tomorrow.
